title: India's Monsoon Is Running 43% Below Normal. The Last Time It Was This Bad, It Set Off a Food-Price Spiral.
excerpt: The Earth Science Ministry says this could be the weakest monsoon in 11 years. Global sugar prices are already surging, Indian markets are wobbling, and 300 districts are on a contingency plan.
body:
India's southwestern monsoon — the single most important weather event for the country's $300 billion agricultural economy — is running at a 43% deficit as of June 26, according to the India Meteorological Department. The Earth Science Ministry has warned this could be the weakest monsoon in 11 years, rattling commodity markets and darkening the outlook for an economy that still depends on rain for nearly half its farmland.

The numbers are alarming. June is ordinarily the key planting window for kharif crops — rice, cotton, sugarcane, and millets — when farmers seed their fields after the first showers pass. With the month nearly over, the monsoon's late arrival and erratic spread have disrupted that calendar in ways that echo an industrial supply-chain breakdown. A super El Niño developing over the Pacific Ocean threatens to make things worse.

## Contingency Plans for 300 Districts

Farm Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan chaired an emergency meeting with state agriculture ministers last week and announced contingency plans for more than 300 vulnerable districts. Of those, 111 have been designated high priority — districts where less than a quarter of farmland has irrigation — and another 76 as medium priority.

States have been advised to push farmers in rain-fed areas toward short-duration, less water-intensive crops such as pulses, millets, and oilseeds. The government has also ordered urgent repairs to ponds, check dams, and other water-harvesting structures.



> **""Markets are consolidating as investors wait to see how India's monsoon progresses."**


"Conditions are favourable for further advance of the southwest monsoon into more parts of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and remaining parts of Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, and Bihar during the next three to four days," the IMD said in its latest forecast. But the deficit through June remains the largest in over a decade.

## Global Markets React


![India Meteorological Department — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f2/IMD_Mausam_Bhavan_Headquarters_New_Delhi_2017.jpg)


The ripple effects are already visible in global commodity markets. Sugar prices surged on Friday, with New York sugar climbing to a two-week high and London white sugar jumping to a 2.75-month high — both driven specifically by fears that weak Indian monsoon rains will cut sugarcane yields. India is the world's second-largest sugar producer, and any meaningful drop in its harvest reshapes global supply.

On Monday, Indian equity markets paused their longest weekly winning streak of 2026. The Nifty 50 fell 0.46% to 23,946 and the BSE Sensex lost 0.48% to 76,728. The auto index dropped 2.1% on fears that a poor monsoon would crush rural demand for two-wheelers, entry-level cars, and tractors.

"Markets are consolidating as investors wait to see how India's monsoon progresses. June rainfall is running at a 43% deficit, and only a pickup in July could revive optimism, given its implications for inflation, demand, and sectors such as autos and consumer goods," said Saurabh Jain, deputy vice president of equities at SMC Global.

## Why the Diaspora Should Pay Attention

For India's 1.4 billion people, the monsoon is not an abstraction. It delivers roughly 70% of the country's annual rainfall and directly shapes the livelihoods of the estimated 600 million Indians who depend on farming. A failed monsoon means lower farm incomes, higher food prices, and increased rural distress — forces that push inflation higher and put pressure on the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy.

For NRIs with family in rural India, the equation is personal. Lower crop yields mean relatives who farm face real income losses. Remittances to farming families — already a critical lifeline in states like Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Punjab — may need to increase this year if July rains do not materialise.

The government has tried to provide some reassurance. India holds ample stocks of staples like rice and wheat, and the contingency plans are more detailed than in previous years. But the El Niño pattern developing in the Pacific suggests this monsoon deficit could widen rather than close.

The next three weeks will be decisive. July typically delivers the bulk of monsoon rainfall, and a strong July can offset a weak June. But if the pattern holds, India may be looking at the kind of agricultural stress that pushes food inflation above 6% — the level that forces the RBI to act, regardless of what global central banks are doing.

*Sources: India Meteorological Department, Reuters, Mint, Barchart*
